name: MAX31855KASA+T
title: MAX31855 cold-junction compensated thermocouple-to-digital converter: seven thermocouple types (K/J/N/T/S/R/E), read-only SPI, 8 SO
summary: A thermocouple interface that measures its own die temperature as the cold junction, converts the thermocouple voltage with a 14-bit ADC and adds the two, giving the hot-junction temperature in 0.25 °C steps as a signed 14-bit word. A 32-bit read-only SPI frame also carries the 12-bit internal temperature (0.0625 °C steps) and three fault flags: open thermocouple, short to GND and short to VCC. Each version is trimmed for one thermocouple type, named by the letter after MAX31855 (K, J, N, T, S, R, E). It runs from 3.0 V to 3.6 V at 900 µA typical, over -40 °C to +125 °C, in an 8-pin SO.

circuits.title: Typical application circuit
circuits.description: The converter reads a thermocouple wired straight to T+ and T- and hands the result to a microcontroller over three SPI lines: SO to the controller's MISO, SCK shared, and CS driven by the controller's slave-select output. A 0.1 µF capacitor bypasses VCC to GND.
notes: A 10 nF ceramic surface-mount capacitor across T+ and T- is strongly recommended to filter noise on the thermocouple leads.

operation.text: Each version is trimmed for a single thermocouple type, given by the letter in the part number (K/J/N/T/S/R/E). Table 1 lists the wire on each input and the nominal sensitivity for every type.

T+ and T- feed conditioning circuitry that cuts noise picked up on the thermocouple leads and scales the signal for the 14-bit ADC. The converted thermocouple voltage gives an uncompensated temperature, to which the measured die temperature is added to obtain the hot-junction temperature. The result may be below the cold-junction temperature.

The die temperature stands in for the reference (cold) junction, so the junction where the thermocouple meets the board should sit at the chip's temperature. The cold end may range from -55 °C to +125 °C. Heat sources placed near the chip cause cold-junction errors.

Within each tCONV the part converts the cold-junction temperature, converts the thermocouple, and runs fault detection, using internal switches S1 to S5. Cold junction: S4 open, S5 closed, S3 (the T- reference to ground) closed, S1 and S2 open. Thermocouple: S1, S2 and S5 open, S3 and S4 closed, so the ADC sees the voltage between T+ and T-. Fault detection: S3, S4 and S5 open, S1 and S2 closed.

The fault circuit checks T+ and T- for a short to VCC or to GND and for an open thermocouple. D2 goes to 1 on a short to VCC, D1 on a short to GND and D0 on an open circuit; all three are 0 otherwise. Any of these also sets D16. With nothing on T+ and T-, D31 reads 0 and D[30:18] read all ones.

Conversions run continuously in the background; the output register updates only while CS is high. Pulling CS low puts D31 (thermocouple sign) on SO within tDV. Each later bit appears within tDO of a falling SCK edge, D[30:18] MSB first. Fourteen clocks read the compensated thermocouple temperature; thirty-two read the whole frame including the reference-junction temperature, which starts at D15. CS may go high at any point in a read.
Conversions begin when VCC passes VPOR, so the first thermocouple result may be invalid with a slow supply ramp; wait tCONV_PU (200 ms) after VCC exceeds its minimum for a valid reading.

Supply noise couples easily into the small thermocouple signal; a 0.1 µF ceramic bypass capacitor close to the VCC pin and to GND reduces it. The input amplifier is low-noise. The thermocouple and its wires belong away from electrical noise sources, and a 10 nF ceramic surface-mount capacitor across T+ and T- filters noise on the leads.
Self-heating can reduce accuracy; its size depends on the package's thermal conductivity, how the part is mounted, and airflow. A large ground plane improves accuracy.

System accuracy benefits from: the heaviest wire that does not conduct heat away from the measured point; thin wire only in the measured region, joined by extension wire through the region free of gradient; freedom from mechanical stress and vibration; twisted-pair extension wire on long runs; no steep temperature gradients; operation well within the wire's temperature rating; protective sheathing in hostile environments; extension wire only at low temperatures and small gradients; and an event log with a continuous record of thermocouple resistance.
